subject: Chemistry
topic: Adding HX and X2 to alkenes
title: Markovnikov's Rule: Addition of HX to Alkenes
summary: Propene + HI gives 2-iodopropane (major) and 1-iodopropane (minor). In step 1 the π electrons of C=C move to the H of HI, forming a C–H bond on the CH₂ carbon, while the H–I pair goes to iodine (I⁻); the + is left on the middle carbon, a secondary carbocation. A 2° carbocation is more stable than a 1° one, so that pathway is favoured, and I⁻ then bonds to it. Markovnikov's rule: H goes to the double-bond carbon with more H atoms, the halogen to the one with fewer.

notes.title: 09 – Markovnikov's Rule: Addition of HX
notes.blurb: the reaction, the two-step mechanism with curly arrows, carbocation stability, the rule and solved examples

keyPoints: Propene is an **unsymmetrical alkene** (CH₂ has 2 H, CH has 1 H); HI is polar, **H<sup>δ+</sup>–I<sup>δ−</sup>**.
**Step 1:** π pair → H (new C–H on CH₂); H–I pair → I (I⁻); the + sits on the middle carbon: a **2° carbocation**.
**2° > 1°:** two carbon groups on C⁺ stabilise the charge; the more stable intermediate is favoured.
**Step 2:** I⁻ gives its electron pair to C⁺: 2-iodopropane.
**Markovnikov's rule:** H → the C with more H atoms; X → the C with fewer H atoms.

blocks.p: The C=C double bond has one **σ** and one **π** bond. The **π bond breaks**, H and I add to the two double-bond carbons, and an **alkyl halide** forms: the **addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes**. Because propene is **unsymmetrical** (CH₂ has 2 H, CH has 1 H), H and I can add in two orientations, giving two products.

Iodine is more electronegative, so HI is polar: **H<sup>δ+</sup>–I<sup>δ−</sup>**. The **π electrons** of the double bond move to the H<sup>δ+</sup> (curly arrow) and form a new C–H bond on the **CH₂ carbon**. At the same time the **H–I pair moves to iodine** (curly arrow), giving **I⁻**. The middle carbon is left with a positive charge: a **secondary carbocation**.
Carbon groups attached to C⁺ help stabilise the charge, so **2° > 1°**. The reaction prefers the pathway through the **more stable intermediate**.
**I⁻** gives its electron pair to the positive carbon (curly arrow), forming the C–I bond.

When an **unsymmetrical reagent** (HX) adds to an **unsymmetrical alkene**, the **hydrogen** goes to the double-bond carbon that already has **more hydrogen atoms**, and the **halogen** goes to the carbon with **fewer hydrogen atoms**. The logic behind it is the stability of the carbocation.
